title: Stentrode endovascular brain-computer interface lets two people with ALS text, shop and manage finances independently at home
summary: Two ALS participants in Melbourne used a Stentrode BCI with ML click decoding for unsupervised home texting, shopping and banking.
account: Two people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and flaccid upper-limb paralysis received the Stentrode, an electrode array delivered through the jugular vein into the superior sagittal sinus at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, in a first-in-human study reported in the Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery (published online 28 October 2020). Participant 1 was implanted in mid-2019 and participant 2 in early 2020; the paper gives no exact dates, so its online publication date is used as the date observed. After machine-learning-assisted training that mapped attempted-movement electrocorticography to mouse clicks, combined with an eye-tracker for cursor navigation, unsupervised home use began on day 86 for participant 1 and day 71 for participant 2. They achieved click accuracies of 92.63% and 93.18%, typed 13.81 and 20.10 correct characters per minute, and independently completed text messaging, online shopping and managing finances. The hospital's statement of 29 October 2020 confirms these activities.
purpose: Restore digital device control for people with severe paralysis without open-brain surgery
system: Synchron Stentrode endovascular brain-computer interface with machine-learning click decoder and eye-tracker cursor navigation
model_version: Stentrode first-in-human system (early feasibility trial, Clinicaltrials.gov NCT03834857)
developer: Synchron Inc. with the University of Melbourne
deployer: Royal Melbourne Hospital (implantation and follow-up); participants' homes (use)
segment: People with ALS and severe upper-limb paralysis

ratings.reason: Two identifiable participants regained independent texting, shopping and financial management at home; because an eye-tracker handled cursor navigation, the BCI's own contribution is the click control, so -3 is not claimed.
First-in-human feasibility in two people; later SWITCH follow-up covered four patients with no serious adverse events, still a small cohort.

ai_role.statement: Per the paper, a machine-learning-assisted decoder (binary SVM or threshold classifier on spectral power) detected attempted movements and generated click commands; cursor navigation came from an eye-tracker, so the AI contribution is the click selection channel, which the authors report with 92-93% accuracy.

evidence.citation: Oxley TJ, Yoo PE, Rind GS, et al. (2021). Motor neuroprosthesis implanted with neurointerventional surgery improves capacity for activities of daily living tasks in severe paralysis: first in-human experience. Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery 13(2):102-108.
evidence.title: Motor neuroprosthesis implanted with neurointerventional surgery improves capacity for activities of daily living tasks in severe paralysis: first in-human experience
evidence.quote: Completion of IADL tasks including text messaging, online shopping and managing finances independently was demonstrated in both participants.

evidence.citation: The Royal Melbourne Hospital (2020). Small brain device proves big game changer for severely paralysed patients. Hospital news statement, 29 October 2020.
evidence.title: Small brain device proves big game changer for severely paralysed patients
evidence.quote: machine learning-assisted training to control multiple mouse click actions, including zoom and left click

evidence.citation: The Royal Melbourne Hospital (2023). Brain interface proves to be safe and effective. Hospital news statement, 24 January 2023.
evidence.title: Brain interface proves to be safe and effective
evidence.quote: This technology holds great promise for people with paralysis who want to maintain a level of independence.

evidence.citation: Mitchell P, Lee SCM, Yoo PE, et al. (2023). Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients: The SWITCH Study. JAMA Neurology 80(3).
evidence.title: Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients: The Stentrode With Thought-Controlled Digital Switch (SWITCH) Study
evidence.quote: At least 5 attempted movement types were decoded offline, and each patient successfully controlled a computer with the BCI.

produced_by: Endovascular electrode array recording motor-cortex ECoG from the superior sagittal sinus
Machine-learning-assisted training of a movement-versus-rest click decoder
Pairing of BCI clicks with eye-tracker cursor navigation on Windows 10
must_hold: Preserved motor cortex activity and suitable venous anatomy
Stable signal bandwidth over months without migration or occlusion
Patient able to use an eye-tracker for navigation

echoes.setting: SWITCH study follow-up of four patients at Royal Melbourne Hospital over 12 months
echoes.source: Mitchell et al. (2023) JAMA Neurology, PMID 36622685; RMH statement 24 January 2023

headline: Stentrode BCI lets two men with ALS text and shop at home
metric: typed 13.81 and 20.10 correct characters per minute

comparator.against: a previous fully implanted BCI requiring burr hole craniotomy
comparator.before: 197 days of training prior to unsupervised home use and achieved a single binary click
comparator.after: unsupervised home use of multiple-click actions within 86 days (participant 1) and 71 days (participant 2) of neurointerventional surgery
comparator.quote: The current study achieved unsupervised home use of multiple-click actions within 86 days (participant 1) and 71 days (participant 2) of neurointerventional surgery.

later.note: The SWITCH study reported four implanted patients completing 12-month follow-up without serious adverse events, and the trial continued in the United States with more participants planned.
later.quote: Each completed 12-month follow-up with no serious adverse events and no vessel occlusion or device migration.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

Replaced 'two men' with 'two people' in the title and account because no cited source gives the participants' sex; added the paper's implant timing (mid-2019 and early 2020) and an explicit note that the publication date stands in for the date observed; renamed the model version to the paper's own registration (NCT03834857) because the JNIS paper never uses the SWITCH name; and treated Mitchell 2023 as independent because its lead and senior authors are Royal Melbourne Hospital investigators.
revisions.source: Oxley et al. (2021) J NeuroInterv Surg, PMC7848062; Mitchell et al. (2023) JAMA Neurology, PMID 36622685; RMH statement 24 January 2023

revisions.change: Added what the benefit is measured against, what happened since from the cited sources.

claim_basis: Two peer-reviewed studies from the makers and two press releases from the deployer are on file. There is no independent source and no finding by a regulator or court.
